utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Krgovic and that we had an explanation yesterday from Mr. Josse. I notice also the absence of Mr. Bourgon who yesterday explained to us that he will be arriving later on in the day. Prosecution, I see Mr. McCloskey. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis for the first part of this sitting. The reason is that Judge Stole is still occupied in the other court case in which he is involved, Haradinaj case. They haven't managed to finish on time so as soon as they finish and he's had a decent break, he will join us. Okay. Mr. Haynes, I understood yesterday that you had agreed with Mr. Bourgon that you will start your cross-examination and then when you finish and he is here, he will proceed and conclude his.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that you understand, I have some questions for you that I think will last about an hour or a little bit more, okay? And then Mr. Bourgon will come back and finish asking you the questions he asked you yesterday. You told us a little bit yesterday about your personal and military background. Would I be right in assume that you have -- you were born and raised and have lived your whole life in the same area of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you have a great deal of knowledge about how things developed in 1992, both before and after the war commenced?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I know about it. I don't know enough. But whatever I know, I am willing to tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that. The village in which you lived, Celopek, was that a Serbian village before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But generally speaking, the municipal area of Zvornik was a mixed area, both Serbian and Muslim, wasn't it, before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was mixed. Percentage-wise, 60 to 40 per cent, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And basically speaking, the ethnic division was village by village, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after war began, each of the villages organised their own defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, every village formed its own units on the territorial principle for one village or group of villages, with a view to protecting their families from the other side. That is what I know about how it was at the beginning in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that the same regardless of whether the village was a Serbian village or a Muslim village, the Territorial Defence was organised in the same way?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Serb territory, but I assume that that was how it was on the other side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But of course, some of these villages that were next to one another had different ethnic populations, so you would have Serbian villages surrounded by Muslim villages, and vice versa, Muslim villages surrounded by Serbian villages, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so these defence systems developed in a way that made the map look like the skin of a leopard; do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain that a little, please, what you mean the skin of a leopard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, a leopard has skin which is substantially one colour but it has spots of another colour so there were areas surrounded by opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the territorial units were being formed for every village, hamlet or group of villages, a certain boundary is established between the Serb and Muslim sides, so that after a certain period of time, the line of separation was sort of formed, and it was a line of defence facing the Muslim forces, and I assume that that was what the opposing side did too. If that is what you meant, that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on. At the start of the war, you were a battalion commander for your village, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't the commander, but I was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It had been from what you told us yesterday, 20 years since you'd had any military experience in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain amount of experience, yes, in terms of organisation and so on, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the other things that complicated, as it were, the situation at the early stages of the war were the return of units of soldiers from the Yugoslav army. Those were the professional soldiers who came to join the forces in Bosnia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The return of forces from other territory partly took place across the territory of Zvornik municipality. Now, which those units were and what their formations were, I really can't remember. I don't have that information, regarding those who passed through coming from other territory. There was some returning forces, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there were also paramilitary units operating in the territory of Zvornik, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning there were some. What they were and how long they stayed, I don't have detailed information, so I can't tell you with precision which forces they were or what size they were, when they were in our territory but I do know that there were some there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they could properly be characterised as just unlawful gangs, couldn't they? They were not under the command of any of the TOs or any army units?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were men or groups of men who probably had certain aims and objectives. I remember a group which came, I don't know exactly whether it was from the area of Uzice or somewhere else. They were taken in but on condition that they place themselves under the control and command of the unit in that area. However, later on, after a day, it emerged that they didn't do that and then the brigade commander reacted immediately and I participated, together with Mr. Nikolic, in telling those men what the order was: Either they would abide and respect all the orders of the battalion commander to whose territory they would be sent or they should immediately go back from where they had come. They were not keen to talk to Mr. Nikolic and me. They wanted to talk to the brigade commander, and they didn't trust us to such a degree that they wouldn't even ride in the same vehicle with us. They came to the brigade headquarters and when they were told that this wouldn't work and that they couldn't behave as they wanted to, they were given a deadline, I can't remember exactly how much, an hour or two, for them to leave the territory, which they did. That is the group I'm familiar with, and I was involved in the activities regarding whether they should stay or leave, and I've just told you what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to finish that off, the brigade commander you're talking about that got rid of these paramilitaries from the territory, was that Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to him becoming brigade commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry, could we clear up the "Nikolic" too?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. The Nikolic you referred to was who?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief for security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, prior to Vinko Pandurevic becoming the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, there had been a large number of previous commanders, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to precisely how many?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise figure but there were several.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about at lower levels, at battalion level? Were commanders of battalions frequently changing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commanders, in the initial stage, and especially by the end of 1992, changed frequently. This applied to both -- especially to brigade commanders, whereas battalion commanders were mostly locals who stayed in those positions until a proper military organisation of the units was established. So regardless when various units were established, the military relationships and hierarchy was not fully established even by the end of 1992. And that is why it was very difficult to change those people who were officers and ordinary soldiers, who were involved in the battalions and the local communities in the territory of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were there many professional soldiers in the Zvornik Brigade after the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade was one of the larger brigades in the area, in terms of numerical strength, as it secured an about 40 kilometre long front. The number, the effectives, changed, but if you're asking me for the figures, I could give you a very rough figures, but not a precise ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like a rough figure because of course you were the assistant to the chief of staff in terms of personnel so you are the person best placed to tell us how many professional soldiers there were as opposed to how many people were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. In that period, that is in 1992, I wasn't what you said. I became that in 1994-1995, but I know that the brigade in that period of time had between four and four and a half thousand men. Later on the number increased, depending on the system, and the way in which the territory was being defended. In the unit, at the beginning, there weren't many professional soldiers, if you're referring to professional commanders from the former JNA, they were very few in number. So that everything depended on the local population, and as I said a moment ago, whenever a new man came, it was very hard for him to take up a duty in the units of any local community, in view of the fact that they -- there was a lot of mistrust. They trusted more their own neighbours, those they knew, than those who were coming from the outside, which was absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic arrived, were the -- was the brigade a better-organised unit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the arrival of Mr. Pandurevic to the position of brigade commander, I wasn't there for quite some time because I was undergoing lengthy treatment, but it is my view, and that of those associates, his arrival meant putting the units into proper military order. This wasn't easy to achieve but the military system of command and control was initiated and established, and I claim that by the end of 1992, or rather up to the end of 1992, there was hardly any proper control and command. It was from the beginning of 1993 that the situation significantly improved and units started to function along military lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And one of the things I want to put to you, you've already answered this, I think, is that paramilitary units were removed from the Zvornik area by Mr. Pandurevic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and described, the previous event, and until Mr. Pandurevic took over, there were several coming and going, but I'm not familiar with the details, but I told you about the case I'm familiar with. I don't know about others. Later on, I don't know that any paramilitary formation came to the territory of Zvornik municipality or within the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on and discuss the job you did towards the latter stages of the war, that you've told us about, when you were assistant to the Chief of Staff for personnel, et cetera. You weren't merely responsible for mobilising men, were you? You were responsible also for requisitioning or mobilising physical objects like buildings and machinery and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever was needed according to establishment in terms of personnel, materiel and everything else went through the department for mobilisation and the requests that came from the Ministry of Defence for the reinforcements that were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Essentially, supplies to the brigade came from two sources, didn't they? They either came from the VRS or they came from the local community?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From both sources, only the amounts, the methods, et cetera, these are things I couldn't be precise about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All technical and military equipment would come from the VRS, wouldn't it, from the rear services of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent it was possible to provide such material, because I assume it was always in short supply, at least that is my view, judging by what I looked like in those days and the others I cooperated with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But for other things, the brigade had to depend upon the local community and the civil authorities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that I said that supplies were provided as available, and this was insufficient for the numbers we had, the local community participated in feeding and equipping the personnel. Now, what the quantities were is something I don't know but I do know that we did receive supplies from the local community. When talking about food, et cetera, and sometimes also financial resources to be given to soldiers to be able to buy whatever they needed for their families, which they were separated from. These were negligent amounts and they were received on an irregular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one particular example before I explore this further. The brigade had certain farm land, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring -- I don't know what land you're referring to. If you mean the area where, in Karakaj, a military farm was established on a temporary basis, yes, it was used for a certain period of time. If you're thinking of any other land, the brigade didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I was referring to that. There was an army farm in Karakaj, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've also heard about another farm at Branjevo but that wasn't the only farm that the brigade had, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also heard about that one. I never went there. It was used for the needs of the battalion which was located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in return for the resources and financial assistance that the local community provided the brigade, were there occasions when civic and political leaders sought to influence the way in which the brigade operated?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because from my position at work, I couldn't tell whether the local community or their representatives did ask for anything in return. This is something I'm not aware of, and I don't know. So I can't answer that question with any precision, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very fair of you. But did local businessmen or civic leaders or people who considered themselves important ever seek to avoid being mobilised in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a question that will be best put to the department of the Ministry of Defence. As for the local authorities and local politicians, whether there were attempts along those lines, I think there were, yes, because I remember, for instance, the reaction of a certain number of personnel in the unit: Why somebody was privileged and was not mobilised? Because apparently the authorities couldn't function without him, whereas others have to go to the front lines, join the units and do whatever is expected of them. So I'm passing on just some views. This was not just me but many people who spent some time in the unit heard these stories and this kind of reaction with respect to those who were not mobilised at all or only for short periods. Therefore, probably there was certain privileges given to individuals so that they could avoid mobilisation. Now, whether the authorities interfered, they probably did, since some people were not mobilised. Nobody could protect me, and that is why I was mobilised, as were thousands of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know what the commander of the brigade's attitude was to such instances where people were not mobilised because of their position or some privilege?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the same attitude towards all the others who were mobilised, as far as I could see during the time period when I was in the personnel service. Because the entire mobilisation went through the service I was working in, therefore the attitude of the commanders towards those who were "protected", and those who were drafted, was the same. He felt it should be all or no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there meetings which members of the brigade attended with the local civic and political authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ever attended a meeting of that sort, whether there were such meetings, I don't know. There probably were. But at any rate, I never attended one, nor did I ever discuss anything with anyone at such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You won't pursue that any further. But can you help us to this? Are you aware whether Vinko Pandurevic was popular with the local civil authorities or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say this: He was more popular among the members of the Zvornik Brigade than with the local authorities. Since I'm a member of the army, I am aware of the sentiment, of the prevailing mood in the army, and I believe that this popularity he enjoyed among the troops is something that could not be equalled or compared to the attitude of the local authorities towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I want to move on now to the process of mobilisation and requisitioning. If, for example, the brigade wished to use a building that belonged to a private enterprise or the local authority, what would be the process that you needed to go through?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A request would be sent to the department of the Ministry of Defence to requisition a certain facility, and that department was in charge of effecting that requisitioning, with prior verification of that facility and its purpose, and if the Ministry of Defence approves it, its representatives go out to inspect the facility together with members of the brigade, and they make their record of the status of the building, the inventory, et cetera, and then after it is no longer needed, those same representatives return, following a certain procedure, the facility to the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that the process that took place, whether the building was required for a long period of time or maybe only a day or two?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every building that needed to be used had to be requisitioned officially, regardless of the duration, because those were private structures, private ownership was guaranteed, and I see no reason why that procedure should be bypassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is that true equally of machinery and vehicles, such as buses or trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to all assets given to the army. Everything the army needs to use and does not own has to be requisitioned and handed over to the army with appropriate records made so that later on, that asset can be returned to the owner, and the legally prescribed procedure had to be followed. The Ministry of Defence is very well aware of that procedure and I tried to describe it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a few documents in a moment but just to set them in context, would each brigade within the Drina Corps have had somebody who did the same job as you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit was formed according to establishment. The establishment envisages all the organs that need to be set up. I know, and I remember, two units of the brigade I belonged to, and in both of them there was a section for personnel, and as for the units of other brigades within the corps, I'm not familiar with them. But if our brigade had such sections within its composition, then I believe that others did too. They may have been called differently perhaps, but they must have had a service to deal with personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I say, we'll see some documents in a minute but equally, the Drina Corps itself would have had somebody charged with requisitioning property on its behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain that term, "requisitioning"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mobilising.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And similarly, the civil police and the MUP, if they wanted to use property, be it a building or a vehicle, they had to obtain a mobilisation order as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the army, in the place where I was. About other organisations, I don't know. Anything that I could say would be pure speculation and I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very fair of you. Just to finish this off before we look at these documents, the purpose of this was that people were who deprived of their property on a temporary basis were entitled to be paid for it, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any remunerations that may have been paid for the use of facilities and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Now, so far as you were aware, and you were the person responsible for it, if the Zvornik Brigade ever mobilised or requisitioned any property for any period of time, it was always properly done by requisitioning order, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was always done. And in that period, I had in my possession a large number of records concerning property we had requisitioned, and after a certain asset was no longer needed, the files were closed, the assets were handed over back to the owner, and the whole file was closed within the Ministry of Defence. But I'm not aware of remunerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to look at about five of these documents with you from the relevant period and I want you to do me a favour, Mr. Galic, in fact, do us all a favour, because these documents are only in your language so I'm going to want to you read out what they are so that those of us who don't speak your language will understand them. They are not very long documents and I'm sure they are very familiar to you but can we look first please at 7D99, please? Is that big enough for you to see, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just first of all, it has your name at the bottom but is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's my name but it's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can see that that's a document dated the 14th of July. Can you read out what it says, please, from the top to the bottom, but sufficiently slowly for the interpreters to interpret what you say?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Military PO box 7469, Zvornik. Confidential number 05/284-1. Date, 14th July 1995. Request for mobilisation submitted to, the section of the Ministry of Defence in Zvornik. For purposes of securing the medical centre in Zvornik, mobilise seven (say seven) military conscripts. The mobilisation is to be effected immediately. Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel, Major Mihajlo Galic." That is the text of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a long time ago. Do you remember making that request?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done in my absence because I was not within the unit that day. This was done by the clerk who worked with me, Andjelko Ivanovic. So this is a document that was sent to the Zvornik department of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Probably my fault, not a very good question, but what I meant was do you remember what the purpose of the request was or did it not come to your attention at all?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document never reached me but I suppose this is a request from somebody in the local community to secure the medical centre. There was a shortage of personnel, and therefore I suppose this request was made to mobilise seven men. That's my assumption because I never -- I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at 7D100, please? You did a very good job last time, Mr. Galic. I wonder if you could read this one out to us again, please, at about the same pace.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, confidential number 01-268, 20th July 1995. Extension of duration of the engagement of the crane requested by the Ministry of Defence, Zvornik department. To meet the requirements of the brigade, extend the duration of engagement of the crane together with operator indefinitely, the crane being the ownership of DD Birac holdings, Zvornik. Signed by Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel, Major Mihajlo Galic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Again the same question: Do you remember making this request and why it was made?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the request. This is an asset that had been requisitioned before, and it was at the disposal of the Zvornik Brigade, for a finite period of time, and since the expiry date was coming close, we sent this request to extend the requisitioning for an indefinite period and that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. A slightly longer document, 7D101, but this one is, in fact, translated. I have a correction to that particular assertion: No, it's not. It is a long document, Mr. Galic, so if you could just read the top of it for us, please, rather than all of it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which beginning? Do you need the preamble, the heading? Where do you want me to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we establish the date, the title and the top paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, confidential number 01-60, 21 February 1994. Performance of tasks in the area of Han Pijesak, order submitted to the commander of the Podrinje detachment." Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the chief of Main Staff of the VRS and the commander of the Drina Corps, strictly confidential number 03/5-98, dated 21st February 1994. Related to continuing combat activities on the axis Pjenovac, Zeravice, Kladanj and the exploitation of success achieved, on the 20th of February 1994, I hereby order..." Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, if you would be so good would you just summarise for us what, as it were, property or manpower is mobilised or is requested to be mobilised by that document?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No personnel is mobilised through this order. It's simply an order to prepare a unit and later probably move it to another territory, to prepare that unit and send it to a certain locality, as specified in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 7D102, please? Again, if you'd be so good, would you just summarise for us what the order seeks to mobilise and the date of it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a second to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of the Drina Corps, confidential number 22/268, 3rd August, 1995, requisitioning of buses and freight motor vehicles, request." This request is in fact an assignment given to requisition buses and freight vehicles. Section Milici, section Bratunac, section of the Ministry of Defence in Zvornik, Sokolac, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, and Srpsko Gorazde, Serbian Gorazde. All of these were given this request or assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And as you've told us, that's a request not by the Zvornik Brigade but by the Drina Corps itself, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One last document, you'll be pleased to hear, Mr. Galic, it's 7D107. And again, if you would be so kind to take a little time to read it and tell us what it is the order seeks, who the order is sought by, and the date of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this copy is not very good, I will do my best. "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, District Staff of Civilian Defence, Zvornik, number 03-137/95, date, 21st July, 1995. "Addressed to the following sections of the Ministry of Defence: Bratunac, Zvornik," the next two are all illegible but I suppose that's Milici and Vlasenica, Sekovici and Kalesija and then added in longhand, Srebrenica. So it was sent to these sections of the Ministry of Defence. "Pursuant to Article," it could be 48 or 49, "and in accordance with Article 36 of the Law on Defence (Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina) and following demonstrated needs, the chief of the District Staff of Civilian Defence hereby orders: "1: Municipal staffs of civilian Defence of Bratunac, Zvornik, Milici, Vlasenica, Sekovici and Kalesija are hereby ordered to mobilise and activate units of civilian defence to clear the terrain and, if necessary, other units of civilian defence for the purposes of clearing the terrain in their own municipalities. "2: The clearing shall be performed in areas free of combat. That is, on terrain that is not exposed to enemy military units. "3: The clearing shall be done with the full cooperation of commands of the VRS. "In the course of clearing the terrain, use the assets and equipment at your disposal. "4:" I cannot read the first line. The second line reads: "Units of civilian defence and those from the list. For purposes of carrying out this order, chiefs of municipal staffs of civilian defence and chiefs of military sections or departments, shall be answerable. And the last line is, "Inform the district staff of civilian defence of Zvornik about the execution of this order. Regularly inform the district staff. Signed by Chief Arsen Krunic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know who that man is, Arsen Krunic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. In fact, I know of him. He is a man who came to Zvornik either from Kladanj or from Olovo where he lived before. I'm not sure which one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just wanted you to tell me what job he did in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the ministry. I think his job had to do with civilian defence. He was chief of that district staff. You can see in the heading that it's from the district staff of civilian defence, concerning these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just one more thing before we leave that document. We can see that paragraphs 2 and 3 begin with the same word, which is "asanacija". Could you tell us what that is, please, and what it entails, what it means?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "asanacija", means clearing the territory from something that could cause epidemics, poisoning, and such things, from anything that should not be preserved in the environment. But what exactly they were supposed to do and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I've done with showing you these documents. I want to ask you this: Schools belonged to local authorities, didn't they, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Elementary schools and the leaderships, that was their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the period in which you've been answering questions about, the period from the 11th to the 18th of July, did the Zvornik Brigade ever seek to mobilise a school at Orahovac, Rocevic, Grbavci, Pilica, Petkovci? ?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor did we mobilise any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about a farm at Agroprom, Branjevo, did it seek to mobilise that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Heavy digging equipment or trucks, were you asked to obtain any such equipment as that during this period?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if such equipment and such buildings were used, it wasn't done through you, through the Zvornik Brigade seeking to obtain them and use them, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a two-part question, and one, the second part I'm not sure he's qualified to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a question I don't need to ask anyway, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on, then, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you briefly about what you know about the activities of Vinko Pandurevic between the 4th and the 15th of July of 1995. You were aware, weren't you, that during that period, he had taken a unit, which we refer to as tactical group 1, to take part in Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. The name I do remember it, but I have forgotten it, but he was absent in the period you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you also aware that the unit which he took to take part in Operation Krivaja 95 was a full battalion plus additional logistical support comprising a unit of 407 men?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual number and the state of the unit is something I do not remember, but that it was a unit in the form of a mini-entity, I don't know exactly how big it was, I don't remember, and I don't know what its numerical strength was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you this: During the period that Vinko Pandurevic was away, the 4th to the 15th of July, did you receive any orders from him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, I did not receive any orders from Mr. Pandurevic on any issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During that period, did you hear from him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't hear from him, not at all, not even once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During that period, did you ever see him in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that period, did you ever hear anybody say they had seen him in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear it, nor do I know that someone else may have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Upon his return on the 15th of July, are you aware that he went to the brigade forward command post at about 1.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the time, but I know according to the combat report, and others, that in the afternoon, I don't know at what time, he was in the field, probably at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were telling us yesterday that the first you heard from him or of him was when you were asked to relay an order to Mijo Dragutinovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, the first you heard of or from Vinko Pandurevic is when you were asked to relay his order. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I didn't hear from him directly but I was passed on this order which I was to relay to Mijo Dragutinovic in the field, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to what time you became aware that you had to pass on that order and what you did with that order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was about 1500 hours n the afternoon. I was tasked to go to the Zlatne Vode region, which is about 2 to 3 kilometres from Zvornik along the old road in the direction of Tuzla, to relay the order to Dragutinovic that the unit that had returned from Srebrenica, after certain tanks refueling, et cetera, that it should move forward and go to the region of the Crni Vrh and Caparde. I passed this on to Dragutinovic and returned to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move to an entirely different topic now just briefly and that's the question of meetings at the brigade command. A number of meetings and types of meetings were held at brigade command, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held at the brigade command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: They varied in size and in the scope of what was discussed. How regularly would there be command meetings held at brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings in the brigade command were held in the morning. Then there was briefing, briefings monthly, with battalion commanders, and other commanding officers. Then there would be occasional meetings of the military personnel for information purposes. I think I have covered all the meetings. I may have left something out. I can't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just in general terms, how many people would attend a monthly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning meetings would be attended by five or six men. Then the briefing with battalion commanders and other units of battalion rank that were independent, there would be about 15. Then meetings with company commanders and independent companies, some 50 would attend. So that would be approximately the numbers I can recall. The numbers of meetings attending -- the numbers of persons attending these various meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you regularly attend these meetings in your capacity as assistant to the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended meetings except when I was in the field, when I was on leave or when I had certain obligations in respect to the Ministry of Defence, when I was sick, when I was undergoing treatment, but in all other instances, if I was in the barracks that day, and if there is a morning meeting, I would attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At any meeting you attended, did you ever hear a discussion about prisoners in schools, executions, burials or reburials?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meetings I attended, and I attended the morning meetings, whenever I was there, except when I was absent, as I said, I would also attend the briefings with battalion commanders and commanders of other units of the same ranks, company commanders, I also attended meetings of the brigade command and the military personnel. This was something that was never mentioned or anything to that effect, at meetings among these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to deal with one small topic and then you'll be glad to hear you can have a break. You will not be glad to hear that I'm going to break my promise to you to be about an hour. I've got a few more questions for you after the break. But I'd like you, please, if you would, to think about the period around about the 17th or the 18th of July when you told us yesterday you first saw Vinko Pandurevic after he came back from Srebrenica and Zepa. You know the period I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want to ask you this: Did he ever issue you with an order that prisoners should be executed rather than taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he issued such an order to me? Never. No one ever issued such an order to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of such an order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I never heard of an order of that kind being issued to anyone in my presence in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Obrenovic ever tell you about such an order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. And whilst I don't say when the breaks occur, I would invite the Chamber to say now is an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could say that without any difficulty at all, Mr. Haynes, but we started at half past 2.00 basically so if you want to proceed for another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, if we have the break now, we'll have the advantage of having Judge Stole join us earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I was go to observe that although we did start at half past 2.00, the witness has been sitting in the chair since quarter past 2.00, so he's been here for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, yesterday when you were being asked questions by Mr. Bourgon, he showed you a plan of the structure of the Zvornik Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And he asked you some questions about the relationship between the commander and the various assistant commanders and chiefs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to summarise, you reported directly to the chief of staff, Mr. Obrenovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And other than the Chief of Staff, there were two assistant commanders, one for logistics and one for religious, moral and legal affairs, and a chief of security?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legal, yes. There were other chiefs there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in relation to those four officers, the Chief of Staff, the assistant commander for logistics, the assistant commander for religious and moral affairs, and the chief of security, did all of them report directly to the commander of the brigade? I should qualify that question; I mean in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As did the other chiefs of services, in addition to those that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about the chief of security? Did he always report directly to the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported to the commander of the brigade, according to the command hierarchy, but as far as I know, the responsibility of the chief of security is also directed toward the superior officer and to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What do you mean by the superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the corps command, depending on the questions involved. I don't know the details but this is prescribed by regulations, acts, orders, instructions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that the position throughout the duration of your service, or did it alter at some stage during the period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that anything was changed. I can't assert one way or the other. I believe that everything was done in the spirit of the regulations in force on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to see if I can refresh your memory a little bit. I'm going to show you a document which is our 7D247. And to alert the court staff to a technical problem, there is a translation of this document but it isn't attached to it. So we'll have to find it before the conclusion of Mr. Galic's evidence. So we'll just have to look at it in Cyrillic at the moment, or in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, the document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then I'll come back do this question. That's the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, if you have the hard copy of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But it can be in e-court in a matter of minutes and I can return to it if that's the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A different topic. Part of your duties, you were telling us yesterday, was to issue death certificates in relation to soldiers who died in the brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just -- not just death certificates but certificates about wounds sustained and certificates about the killed members of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it was also part of your duty to keep a review of losses in combat, of soldiers in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers were recorded in the service I was working in. As for the names and all particulars of the losses were kept by the department for morale, religious and legal affairs. These two departments always had identical data, in terms of numbers and the particulars, names, surnames, and every other particular, of the fighters killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you agree that the brigade commander does not know the reality of battle losses until some days or weeks after the losses occur?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of combat activities, it was not possible to have precise information on losses, who were wounded lightly, more seriously, those killed, missing, et cetera. These reports certainly reached the commander eventually but the precise figures were available only once those activities were completed, that is a day or two or maybe three days later, if the operation was a major one. And after such operations, the brigade commander does have, and had to have, precise information on all losses suffered by the unit, which were collected from the units that took part in combat operations and their commands. These were collected and then the official and complete information was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've heard in this case some evidence about the combat activity that took place in the area of Baljkovica on the 16th of July. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the testimony, but I do remember the information that reached me and the department for morale linked to the losses that were suffered on that day in Baljkovica. As part of the total losses of the Zvornik Brigade had in the period from 1992 to 1995 or, rather, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to explore with you, as it were, the developing state of the command's knowledge as to the losses at Baljkovica. But before we do that, I'd like you to explain to us some of the reports that the brigade command would issue on a regular basis. It's right, isn't it, that on a daily basis, a daily combat or regular combat report was sent by the command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on occasion, though not always, an irregular or interim combat report would be sent by the command to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called it, according to military terminology, an extraordinary combat report. That is also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to who would prepare, who would write, those documents?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular operational reports were written by the duty operations officer in the brigade command, whereas the interim combat reports were drafted by the officers who thought it was indispensable to send such reports to the superior command. So I can't tell you precisely whether it was the commander, the chief of staff, the chief of a certain department, but these regular daily reports compiling all the information about events that took place that day were prepared by the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct also that the regular or daily combat reports tended to be sent at more or less precisely the same time every day?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- it was clearly stated when such reports should be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We are going to look firstly at a regular or daily combat -- no, we are not. We are going to look at an irregular or extraordinary combat report from the 16th of July, and I'd like to put into e-court for you to have a look at now, please, Mr. Galic, P330. Is that big enough for you to read?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that an irregular combat report for the 16th of July of 1995, sent by the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the superior command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an extraordinary report. Can I see the signature? I can't see the whole report. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no signature. This was just signed with the rank, commander, and the first and last name, because this is a document that was sent through the communications system. They must have received a document that was signed. This is just the text that was encoded -- in coded form sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I wonder if the document could be brought -- I'm bound to get it wrong -- down or up. I want to see the second part of paragraph 2, please. Now, does this report contain information as to the number of dead that had been -- the number of deaths that had been sustained by the brigade according to the belief of the command at that time on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it? I see that it's written in combat we had dozens of men wounded, about ten dead, and five gone missing. We shall provide more precise information later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's enough. That's all I want you to read. The information as to the number of dead, as the command believed it to be at the time this message was sent. And I think if we go to the bottom of the document again we will see the time at which it was sent. I wonder if you could help us as to that? Does it say 1810 or 10 past 6.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see a stamp, and the signature of people who were doing the encryption, and it says, "Due to the bad condition of the relay, the telegram was repeated several times," and the times are indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just help us with the times so that we can have them on the record? I think there is 1758, 1810, and then 2005. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as we were saying earlier, of course, the reality of battle losses are not always immediately available or available to the commander but we can see that by the evening of the 16th of July, the command thought they had lost ten men. Let's have a look at how the information they had developed over the next few days. Can we have a look at P331, please? Can you read that, Mr. Galic, or is it too faint for you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You can read it all to yourself and those of us who speak English can read it in English but I'm going to -- if you read it through to yourself I'm going to ask you if you agree with this: This is a regular combat report from the 17th of July and it shows no losses at all, doesn't it? And I think you'll need to look at paragraph 7 in the document. Can the document be taken down for -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. I cannot see which paragraph it is. I see item 7, 8 and 9, the three last ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 7 is the one at the top of the page now. Are you able to read that for us?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that it shows no losses at all?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to make it out, but I can't make out the first four words, so no losses are shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and read it to you. It says, "There were no casualties. We will send you a more detailed information on previous events in a supplementary report." And again, could you tell us at what time that document was sent? What time was that document sent?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- could you show the entire stamp, 17 July, 1995, at 1920 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So it appears from this that by 20 past 7.00 on the 17th of July, the command of the Zvornik Brigade still thought they had only lost ten men. I want to go to P334 now, which is an irregular combat report from the 18th of July. And to help you, you're going to have to look, I think, at paragraph 3 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the paragraph. Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That would be very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In combat with Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Zepa and with the stragglers and the forces of the 24th and 25th infantry divisions of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade sustained the following losses: Dead, 27 conscripts; seriously wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's all I'm interested in. But by the 18th of July, the state of knowledge of the brigade as to the number of dead it had suffered was that there had been 27 people killed, but that included the action at Srebrenica, the action at Zepa, and all other combats with the 2nd Corps and the 24th and the 25th divisions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is written in that -- in this report, in item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see if we can work out how many people died at Srebrenica. We can look at P321 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have an objection to him putting his case through this witness and as opposed to calling the witness back but there should be some connection between this witness and the testimony, and just going through documents this witness is not aware of or connected to is my objection. If he can connect it no problem but I think we are just going through documents and he's agreeing with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He's the chief -- assistant chief of staff for personnel. He told us yesterday he signed death certificates. On August the 21st of last year, Mr. McCloskey opened his case on the basis that 50 men had died at Baljkovica on the 16th of July. I want to put the evidence straight about that. And this is the best witness to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see any basis for your objection, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Haynes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was just going to ask the witness to look at P321, if we can. And we are going to need to scroll down, where I think you'll find some names. The following page, please. Again, it's a faint paragraph 7. Can you see five names there, and a bit of text above it? Would you read that out to us, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "As a result of combat activities executed in the area of Srebrenica, the following men were killed in our brigade: Dragan Nikolic; Djuro Ubiparipovic. Zoran Dukic. Milisav Micic. Radovan Ostojic." With the father's name indicated for each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were any of those men known to you, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see under number 4, this young man from my home town who was killed. I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But according to that report, which is a report from the 11th of July, five people died at Srebrenica, and if my mathematics is correct, that should suggest that the brigade lost 22 people in all other combats, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report and this information, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want you to see one more document, which is 3D56, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a list of the fighting men from the Zvornik Brigade who were killed. It was prepared by this section for morale, religious and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And next to each name on the far right-hand side, does it give the date and place where they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Against each name we see the date of birth, the date of death, and the place of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you know, because you've looked at this before, that this is a document that runs to 20 pages, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the document. I don't know the number of pages. But I did hold this document a thousand times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'm going to have you handed now a hard copy of this document, and I've got copies for everybody. Now, one of the occasions when you handled this document before was when you and I went through it together the other day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did we highlight in the document the occasions or the people who had died at Baljkovica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's highlighted in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to short circuit it, it matches up with the other document we've seen because we find 22 people died at Baljkovica, three on the 15th, and 19 on the 16th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tacno or not tacno is -- Mr. Haynes, on page 12, for example, number 6 from the top, he also died allegedly, Vaso Novakovic in Baljkovica. Yeah, but that's on the 30th, that's 1993. And there is another one on 1992, on page 14. So you're restricting yourself to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm restricting myself to the battle that is relevant to this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to complete this picture by showing you a couple of other documents which illustrate a different point, and that's P325. If we could just go down to the bottom part of this document, and a bit further, all I'd like you to do quickly, and we can do it by reading the document as well as anything else, is to confirm that no losses were reported to the corps command on the 13th of July, and if we look quickly at P326, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, have you seen -- are you familiar with this document already? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it before, but even now I don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is why I pointed it out, because if he's looking at what I am looking, then obviously he cannot see it. We did have it in the initial stages. We had the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It needs to go up to the previous page in the Serbian version, and he needs to look at paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your attention is directed to that one sentence in paragraph 7. If you could read it out aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As a result of an enemy shell, one soldier was slightly shell-shocked. He remained in the unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like to go on now, please, quickly to P326. My guess is it's going to be paragraph 7 again.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. "In the past reporting period, there were no men wounded lightly or seriously."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And by whom is that document apparently sent?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent by Chief of Staff Major Dragan Obrenovic, to the command of the superior staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It probably follows from the other documents we've looked at as to the total numbers of dead but Mr. Obrenovic did not, on the 13th or the 14th of July, apparently report any lost men at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't see it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm finished with that particular topic. Would you just bear with me one minute, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to the topic I left a few minutes ago and ask if you can now be shown 7D247, please. Firstly, have you seen a document like that before? Or have you seen that document before, would be a better question.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this document before, but I heard that it had reached the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to read it out but what was the effect of that document and what date does it originate from?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 24th of October 1994. It came from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and it relates instructions concerning command and control over security intelligence organs of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what instruction did it give? Did it change an existing situation in any way? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed one thing, and I think that probably this instruction clearly defined certain activities that were not properly conducted before. It was necessary to clarify whether it was necessary to send two combat reports or only one. I didn't know exactly in which month it was sent but we were told that this instruction had arrived and that it stipulated that two reports should be sent to the superior command: The regular operations report and one report made by the security organs. After that, there was no longer any ambiguity or any problems. It was done according to instructions, if that is the content of what I'm just seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to leave that with you, Mr. Galic, and perhaps take it up some other time. Just one last topic, you'll be glad to hear. And it's about being a duty officer. It's correct, isn't it, that there was a duty officers' rota at brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that the duty officer would change every 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that generally speaking, the changeover would occur at about 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, at the commander's office, or the chief of staff's office, if the commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would there be effectively a night watchman to deal with the night-time and a duty officer who was there during the day?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, there were a number of documents available to the duty officer. I want to ask you about a couple of them. One was known as the duty officer's notebook, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the duty officer's notebook would record important messages for the commander or the chief of staff, whoever was in charge of the brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sorts of information were entered in that notebook, not only concerning the commander. Even private messages were entered there, if a family was trying to contact someone who was not there at the moment. There was no stipulated procedure. There was no strict procedure concerning what could be entered. The duty officer would enter all sorts of information and, as I said, that sometimes included private telephone calls from families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One of the things that the duty officer had to be aware of was the whereabouts of the commander at any particular time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Or the deputy, if he's outside the zone of responsibility on any business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That would even include if the commander or the deputy was on personal business. There would be some record of how to contact him, wouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me point out that it was customary for both of them to open the door of the duty officer and tell him, "From now until such and such a time, I will be in a certain place, and you can reach me at this phone number." And he would leave. And that is all the duty officer would know. That was how both Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Obrenovic acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm going to very quickly show you one example of that, and it's 7D138 in e-court. In the middle of that page, you see a phone number, 589-991, and next to it komandant or K'dant. Do you know where a 589 number would be in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know which area is covered by this telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And are you familiar with that number that was left there in relation to the commandant on the 26th of June apparently?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a number, though it is hard to say now, and to interfere in anyone's privacy. I'm at court, so this is the number of a friend of Commander Pandurevic, and he would drop in there. And that is why that number is noted. If the need should arise, that he could be called up. And it is about two to two and a half kilometres away from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it a man or a woman friend?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A woman friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to move briefly on to another document that was kept at brigade command, and that's the diary of the duty operations officer. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the document on the monitor now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, it's not the document on the monitor now. It's another document. It's the duty operations officer's diary. Do you remember that document being at brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make something clear. The diary of the operations duty officer, and the one in the barracks, so will you ask me which exactly you are asking me about, the duty operations officer, the duty office in the barracks, and then there was the barracks commander and that was not Mr. Pandurevic. And then there was the duty operations officer. So I'd like to know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a very fair question of me and I want to know about the diary of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it, but I'd like to see what you're going to show me for me to be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before I do that, I'd just like to know what the duty operations officer would record in that book or document. Would he similarly record the comings and goings of the commander or the komandant?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume he would. I have a report in front of me with notes by the duty operations officer, says, "Palma, situation regular, Draga to call up Milosevic, Stanevic, Milos, Pero [phoen] From Sokolac." He asked for Milosevic, deal with the problem of sick leave of officers, in regular combat reports, et cetera. These are the observations made by the duty operations officer in the course of the day, and reports from the field are collected together and then forwarded to the superior command. Clearly it doesn't have any particular format. These are just notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I'm really seeking to ask you is whether the document that you have in front of you, which is the duty officer's notebook, and the other document I'm referring to, which is the diary of the operations duty officer, would contain similar information about the whereabouts of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might find it in the duty operations officer's book. The barracks commander would not keep a record of such things. And there was no need for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to cut to the chase here. Could you have a look, please, at our 7D207? This is an entry for the duty officer's notebook from the 16th of September. Can we go down this page, please? Would you see the entry, the third asterisk up from the bottom? And read that over to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vinko Pandurevic" -- this is smudged so I can't see what it is. I can't read it. It's illegible. "Vinko Pandurevic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I'm going to do -- is that better for you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's larger but it's still not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see the time at the end, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I'm going to suggest to you [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Haynes, seems to have -- now it's on. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I believe the English translation to be is Vinko Pandurevic returned back at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that now. "Returned at 11.30." It's not -- I couldn't see very well because of the lines on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just bear with me a second. Mr. Galic, I'm very sorry I took so long with you having said I'd only be an hour but I'm finished now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, regarding 7D247, which you said -- you were told at the time was not yet on e-court, then eventually we saw it, have you traced also the English version of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
