utterances.text: We believe the position is this: Mr. Bourgon helpfully turned around and says that it looks as though the Nikolic Defence team have put it into e-court in both of its forms as well so maybe we can sort that out before the end which will save us having to locate the English translation which, as I understand it, is in e-court under a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We found it and sent it to you folks. So you've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. That's very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Bourgon, would you now please conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The number I was indicated to my colleague is 3D124, which is on e-court is the English translation of the document they were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a few more questions to ask of you today, and I will try to proceed as quickly as possible. First, you said yesterday, and I'd like you to confirm, that you did at times act as operational duty officer during the period from June to September 1995. Can you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations duty officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how often did you act as operational duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know. But according to the schedule. I can't remember exactly when and in what order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if I say to you, Mr. Galic, what kind of frequency? Was it regular? Was it something that you did only once or twice? Can you add any -- can you give us any information as to the frequency that you would be the operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A slight clarification, we have IKM and brigade so he knows which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, the witness understood and he corrected me by saying operational duty officer. We are referring to the Zvornik Brigade command. We are not referring to IKM. And I believe the witness understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. But the gentleman is also right. I said that I was on duty according to the schedule. Now what that schedule was like, I can't remember. Was it once a fortnight, once a month, twice, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. If you would receive -- when you were on duty -- first of all, you -- of course, my colleague asked you some questions and my understanding is that you would have to complete both the operational duty officer's notebook as well as the duty officer diary. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To write down information in the diary of the operational duty officer and the diary of the officer on duty? These are two separate notebooks. The operational duty officer makes notes in one of those documents, and the other document, entries are entered by the duty officer in the barracks in that other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back and I'll show you some documents like this. Now, my colleague shared with you information that would go into the operational duty officer's notebook. And what I'm interested in is if you would receive a phone call during your period of duty, I take it that would you write the name of the individual or of the unit, followed by a dash, and then you would write the information obtained from that person or unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends how the information is being conveyed. If it's by telephone, I don't know whether the duty operations officer will note it down or not, whether he's retained it in his memory or not. It all depends. I don't know how I can answer that question. Logically, he should make note of it. Now, whether each one of them did or not, I don't know. Because this applies to me too. The operational duty officer, as we have seen, sometimes notes everything, sometimes not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Galic. Let's look at a few examples. I'd like to call up on e-court, 3D126. Now I have to say that this is a Defence document which is part of P377. So it needs to be opened but with 3D126. And there is a translation included therein, and that's the translation I would like to use, the second translation. And I believe this was prepared at the break. I'd like to go to English page 6, as well as B/C/S page 13. And to have both on the screen, please. Mr. Galic, I will ask to you to look at the document before you, where you see the word "Livada". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Livada, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, beside Livada, there is a dash and then it says, "Situation normal." Now, would I be right in saying that this refers to information which was received from Livada?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the word also in the same document, where it says, "MAD," or mike-alpha-delta, it says "MAD" then there is a dash, and in English it says, "Has executed the order to raise the level of combat readiness." Now, my understanding -- do you see the word "MAD" at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my understanding is that this is information which was received from the mixed artillery battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move, keeping the same document, I'd like to move to English page 11 and B/C/S page 18, and I draw your attention, Mr. Galic, to the first entry on this page. Do you have it on the English and we now have it in your language. Now, the first entry, if you can read it for yourself, and the other -- in the courtroom, we have the English version and my understanding is that this is information which was received by the Zvornik Brigade operations duty officer, and that this information was received from the security officer present at the forward command post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I say on the basis of what, whether this is the duty operations officer, the duty officer? I really find it difficult to take a position when shown such documents. It's very hard for me to look at each of these documents to say whether it was written by this or that person. You must know that I didn't know all ten or 15.000 soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade and how they write their notes. I'm just a participant who does not have such memory able to keep all that this my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, is this information which was received by the operations duty officer? Please say yes or no. Was this information received?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it can be in the book and it wasn't received by the Zvornik Brigade operational duty officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's told you that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make sure he's reading the very sentence, the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, I draw your attention to the first entry at the top where it says the letters I-K-M for forward command post, security, dash, and then it says that they -- that they are coming from behind Krizevici and there is shooting at SO Potocari. Do you see the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now what I say, Mr. Galic, is --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what you had just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The following: I suggest to you that this is information which is coming from the security officer who is present at the forward command post. This page refers to the 14th of July. And what I'd like to know is can you tell me which of the two Zvornik Brigade security officers was with you at the IKM on the 14th of July, if any.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was with me at the forward command post on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what do you make of this entry in the operational duty officer notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to -- what to make of it. The duty operations officer, if we look at this, who wrote it and how, we see two quite different handwritings, I simply cannot comment on this, and cannot give you any answer, whether the duty operations officer received this or not, I don't know, I can't judge on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm asking. If you don't know, please just say so and we'll move on. I'd like to move on to page 19 in English and page 26 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. I mean, just in case I am right, but in the English text, in the second line, we have SO Potocari. In the transcript, when you read it out, also we find that you stating SO Potocari. Was it Potocari or Potocani? I can't really decipher --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping]... Translation besides I'm not sure if I can make whether it's Potocari or Potocani. I would guess it's Potocani but to be honest this is not really my point today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning in case it can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can enlighten us on that. You can see the text, the handwritten text in your own language on the screen. The third line, where you have SO, is it Potocari or Potocani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Potoca" -- and then there is a squiggle that doesn't look like any letter. It says "Potoca" and then I can't read that letter either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can we -- is this entry dated on the previous page, Mr. Bourgon? Is this entry, this particular entry, dated on the previous -- on any of the previous pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, on the previous pages and it's dated 14th of July and that's what I put to the witness. It's not on this page but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. So this was page -- this was English -- this was English 11 so can we go to English 10? And we'll have to scroll back. I don't know exactly. I think we have to go to page 8 in English to see the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back page by page until we find the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah. And this is page 8, Mr. President, and on top we see 14 July and the information. Then we can move with the same size if we can now to page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's quite a bit more foundation that you'll be hearing about dates and how this book is dated so I would just before we get there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop, stop. All right. I just wanted to know whether from the document on the face of it there appears a date or not. And you've indicated page 8 as containing the date of the 14th of July, assuming that there is a sequence after that, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on now to page 19 in English and page 26 in B/C/S. Now, Mr. Galic, this entry is still on the 14th of July, and I'd like to see if you see something here that concerns you in this book.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what does that --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Galic should mobilise all able-bodied men." It's written in capitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The indication in the book is that this is the 15 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, my mistake, it is 15 July. It is my mistake. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you both. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to now move to the forward command post, operations duty log, and I'd like to call up on e-court P347. And I'd like to move immediately to English, page 6 -- English page 6 and B/C/S page 8. Now, you will see from the document that will come up, Mr. Galic, that this is where you recognised your handwriting yesterday, but before I ask you questions on this page, I have one more question before that. In your second interview with the Prosecution, and I'm not going to show it to you unless you insist, on page 5 and in B/C/S on page 9, there was a question which was put to you by the investigator, which is: "Had you served as a duty officer at the forward command post before?" And your answer was: "Yes, like all other commanding officer and officers, we had our duties, regular shifts, regular shifts at the forward command post or twice a month." My question is very simple: Do you understand what I just mentioned, that comes from your second interview with the Prosecution -- first?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is simple: How do you reconcile this answer which you gave to the investigator during the second interview, meaning regular shifts and duties like all other commanding officers, with your first interview where you said you had little to do with such things? How do you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first interview, I don't believe I said quite that, the way you put it. I was the operations duty officer according to the schedule, as well as a duty officer on the forward command post according to schedule. I couldn't have said anything else. Now, when I was there, I can't remember. Unless we look at the notebook and see what the schedule was. We discussed this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's make it easier, Mr. Galic. Let's go to 3D116. I'm sorry for the Court usher, just to 3D116, page 5 in English and page 9 in B/C/S. So you can see exactly what you said to the investigator during the first interview. Sorry, it's not 3D116, it's 3D115, the first interview. So we have 3D115 in English on the left and now we'll put up in your language on the right. If we can scroll down the English on the left, please. Let's move on because I don't want to waste any time in looking at this. My question, Mr. Galic, is the following: In your second interview, you described that being on duty was a regular matter, whereas in your first interview you said you had little to do with being -- anything that has to do with duty officers. My question is quite simple: How do you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, he's asked for the statement about "little to do with". I didn't see it. I know it's hard to find this stuff sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey is perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will come back, Mr. President, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the documents I asked earlier which was the forward command post log, and that was P347, and to go English page 6 and B/C/S page 8. Now, you have before you, Mr. Galic, on the right side in B/C/S, that is the -- what you saw yesterday, and you recognised your writing where it says 13 July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to move to --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- the top of this page, and I'd like you to look at the headers on the top of this page. First I'd like to go back to page 5 first, please. Page 5, English and page 7, B/C/S, sorry. What I'd like you to look at, Mr. Galic, is the top, the headings which go with the columns and what we see is that there are six columns with the following headers, number, date and time, contents, officer taking over duty, officer handing over duty, and finally there is a row and can you tell me what this word is, the sixth column that is there at the end?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Primedba" which means remarks, observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. President, I'd like to note that in the English version the sixth column is not there and it should be there. It's simply missing, it's the column with remarks. Now, I'd like to move, if you can look at this was the page which was immediately, if we scroll down please on the B/C/S version, which says, 12 July 1995. Can we now move to the next page, English page 6, B/C/S page 8? Now, I will ask you to look at this document and confirm that in this document also, there are six columns, and even though there are no headers at the top it follows the same model as the previous page, with the six columns being number, date, time, content, taking over duty, handing over duty, and remarks. Do you see this, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I see those columns, though we can't actually see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'd like simply to make a reference that the two pages I've just shown, which are in English page 5 and 6, in the original book are side by side, and my colleague can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move now to the next page, which is 7 in English and 9 in B/C/S. And I'd like you to comment on the new headings or the headings which appear at the top of this page, which is the page that you filled in.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Date, time, content, officer taking over duty, officer handing over duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you go back to the beginning, if we can scroll to the left -- to the right, sorry, we can see at the beginning there is no longer a column with number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. It doesn't say number? What number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We can go back to the previous page where the first column was the number of the entry, and in this page, now, can we go back one page on the B/C/S side, on both sides, go back one page? Sorry, that was the right page, sorry, we had the right page. If we can go back to the page with the 15th? Now, if we can just leave it like this, you see the headings at the top, is that your writing, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'm saying to you is whereas before, we had six columns with the first column being number and -- of entry and the last being remarks, we have now moved to a new format with five columns, with the date, the time, the contents and in and out. There is no longer any remarks column. There is no longer a column with number. My question is: If this is your writing, then why did you change the format of the book on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at all why, nor is there any reason. What is important here is the date, the time, the description of activities of the people who were on duty and who replaced each other. I see no reason why it should be this way or that way. There is no prescribed way of doing it. It's just a notebook in which lines were drawn, tables, and these data were entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the previous page, on both English and the B/C/S, we will see that there was an entry number there. And I draw your attention beside 13 July 1995, you put a number 8 there. And if we go back one page before that, on both sides, both the English and the B/C/S, we see the entry numbers in the book, where you have entry number 6, entry number 7, the following page is where you put entry number 8, and then the page I referred you to there are no longer entry numbers. I'm asking you why did you stop putting entry numbers if this is your writing? Can we go back to the page which has 15 July which is -- why did you change the format and why is there no longer entry numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can go back one page, now we see here in the English version that there is a separation line between the 13th and the 14th, but in the original version, there is no separation line there. As a matter of fact, the separation line is the one that is on top of the entry of the 13 July. Now, seems logical to me there should be a line between 13 and 14. Why did you not put a separation line there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I don't know, and don't know what that is supposed to mean, if my duty continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move to the next page? In the same manner here, between the leftover of the 14 July which is at the top of the page, and the 15th of July, where you have 0445, you did not put a line to separate the days. Is there a reason why you did not separate those days like everywhere else in this book the dates are separated?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on duty on the 15th of July until 7.00 in the morning. These activities happened at 0445. And I probably -- I had already written there what the units from the ground informed me as to what was going on, and that's probably the reason why this was not underlined. But a line was drawn when I turned in, and others replaced me on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question, Mr. Galic, is if you look where you signed in this book, you signed in the column beside 15 July as the officer taking over duty. Why is it that after changing the format of this book, you signed in this column and not in the column which says officer handing over duty?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only place in that column where I could have signed. I see no other reason. You're asking me things that -- all this related to activities while I was on duty. I could have signed in the beginning, in the middle, at the end. I don't see why I would have signed at the bottom or on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we see, Mr. Galic, that the next entry after the 15 July is the 21 of July. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the column 21 July, what I'd like to know is how come you did not sign the column for the officer handing over duty on the 15th? Why did you not sign officer handing over duty? I'm referring to you the 15th of July, 4.45. You sign as taking over and you did not sign as officer handing over the duty on the 15th. And I suggest to you, Mr. Galic, that the reason is that, in fact, there was no one to take over the duty from you because you were not sitting in the IKM when you wrote these entries.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I believe that this book was the only one on the ground. In fact, it was only there -- other books were at the command, and it was written up there at the IKM. It certainly wasn't written in the command or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can go back one page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are informed that Mr. McCloskey wishes to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Bourgon have been talking about a topic that's come up. We both agree it's -- like for the witness to see the original book, the original IKM book. But I just flipped it open and the page that Mr. Bourgon is challenging is hanging on to the binding by a thread. It's about to come off and before that does come off, I would like it if the Court would take a look at it because if it comes off, it will then be separate from the binding. And I had not anticipated this challenge, I will admit, but we have the book. You can see it. I think it's something you ought to see. It's very unusual but I think it's something worth looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put us in a very delicate position because if I touch it and the page comes off, it will be my fault. So I don't know who to delegate in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I tried to ask Janet Stewart. I can bring an investigator down as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We fully agree, Mr. President. It will be a good thing if you can look at the book very quickly and after that maybe I wouldn't be surprise that you will ask for the book to be given to you and signed over to you at some point to look at it because it's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing. How much more time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can finish today if we don't take too much time to look at this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there are others who may wish to cross-examine this witness, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not cross-examining him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who would like to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no cross-examination at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking who would like to, who wishes to, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Miletic will have a relatively short cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are we to expect a re-examination, too, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- all right. Let's bring this notebook or logbook and have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's right here. I don't know where you want to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's so fragile that if it's moved, that would bring the calamity you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think it's a calamity but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the page that says 13 July. If I could show it to you, I think that would be a good thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you come forward -- we need to see. Why don't you both come forward and let us see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. I think Madam Usher, you may proceed to bring in the witness. We are waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to go on the record to say what everyone observed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can do that. We were shown in the meantime the logbook. The page of the entry relative to the 13th of July is already loose. The page which contains the entry of the 13th of July is hanging by a thread, as it was put to us, and could come loose, become loose anytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and just the page that on 13 July that's hanging loose is ERN 00760275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, let's go on so I can finish my cross-examination today. I'd like to go on the -- I will ask the usher to give you the original of the forward command post logbook so that you can put it beside you on the ELMO and look at it. And I will draw your attention to the page which has the number 274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, the pages are coming loose now. If you are not careful, that page, which is just hanging to the binding by a thread, will come loose. If you can preserve it in its current position, we would appreciate that. The same applies to Madam Usher, if she can follow what I am saying. Yes. All right. Now, we look at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can get Madam Usher to show the -- this page but to go up so that we can see the beginning of entry number 7, sorry, go down, we can see the beginning of entry number 7, which is the 12th of July. Do you see this, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the columns beside where it says "officer taking duty" and "officer handing over duty", there is no one signing in those two columns. If we can just move the book to the left so we can get the next page where we see 13th of July and 14th of July, and if we can move the book down so that we can see the top part, again, please, the -- completely down, down and then left, sorry, up and left. I'd like the top of 275 -- no, left. Yes, this. Now, Mr. Galic, you see here that -- where we have the top part of page 275, this is the follow-up of day number 12 of July, at least this is what it appears to be. Do you agree with that? It's a follow-up to the officer on duty on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I said to you is that if you look beside, in the columns of handing over duty and giving over duty, you see that someone signed where it says officer handing duty for the 12th of July but there is nobody who signed beside for the entry where you put your writing for the 13th of July. Now, my question is the following. It appears by looking at this book that there was no one who took over the duty from the person who was there on the 12th of July. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we move to the next page, if we turn the page and we go to page 276, flipping the page over, and we look at page 276, now, also, if you look in the book, Mr. Galic, you can look in the original if you want. Maybe that's better for you. If you look at the book where it says 15 July and 21 July, it appears that there is no one who took over from you on the 15th of July. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that he didn't take it over but it's just not recorded in the book. Duty was certainly taken over, and in the course of the 15th, there was a duty officer at the forward command post and the commanding officer was already on the forward command post on the 15th. Why it wasn't written --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, if there was an officer on duty who came in on the 15th, he did not sign where it says officer taking over duty. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 15th of July, yes. I'm not sure if I said --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody signed as taking over duty. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that be -- where -- because the box where it says officer handing duty, I take it that because you didn't sign that column, that means that you did not meet the officer who took over duty from you on the 15th. Do you recall meeting someone to hand over duty on the 15th? I'm asking for your memory, not what is in the book.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and I've already said so several times, that Major Ljubo Bojanovic took over duty from me. Why he didn't sign for it, why he didn't enter it, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I won't get back on your previous interviews but in your interviews and it is my intention to file the statements with the Court, you did not remember who took over duty from you in your second interview. So I just ask that if you know today that Major -- that Major Bojanovic took over duty from you it is because you learned that fact later on and you did not know when you had your second interview. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already asked you to try to understand that I didn't have any documents to remind me, and I couldn't recall the dates and in the same way this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have to stop you because I'm talking of the second interview where you were shown the book and you said to the investigator that you did not remember who took over duty from you. Now, I'm going to stop here and move on to my next question, and I'm simply asking you, according to this book, you came on duty the 13th of July and you stayed until the 15th of July. My question is: Did you inquire as to why you were staying on duty so long at the forward command post when the normal shift was 24 hours? Did you complain to anyone about this fact?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not complain. First of all, I had no one to complain to that day. Secondly, I was there only 23 hours on the 13th, in the morning, and from the 14th until 15th, in the morning, that was my normal, regular shift on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we will talk about your regular shift, Mr. Galic. I'd like now to move to page in B/C/S page 10, and in English -- sorry, just in English, page 8 on the e-court and I'd like you, Mr. Galic, to look at the page which bears the number 277. On the left side on the e-court can we move to the next page, 277? Now, Mr. Galic, on this page, 277, would that be your writing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So then you were again on duty on the 21st to the 22nd of July, after being on duty on the 15th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this case, it appears that you signed in the officer handing over box and that there was in fact someone who was there to take over duty from you on the 23rd and who signed in the right place. Do you see that in the book?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the screen, no, but in the notebook, yes, I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the notebook, in the original and where we will follow you on the screen and you can look at the original, with the page 277. You see that you signed as officer handing over duty and that someone took that duty over from you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can come back one page back to page 276? Now, in this case, you did not sign on the 21 of July, there is no signature with this officer whereas you say as officer taking over duty. How come you did not sign in that box where it says officer taking over duty?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your second interview, Mr. Galic, you did not recognise that signature in the box of the officer handing over duty; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise it now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, unless, of course, the officer who signed as the officer handing duty, there is a possibility, of course, that he handed over duty at 21 July in the morning at 6.00. Now, this, of course, would mean that when you wrote the entry on the 22nd July, there was no one to take over duty because you were not at the IKM when you wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I can explain this. If I'd known that I needed someone to represent me here, I would have asked for it. I really don't know how I can prove to you that I was there at the forward command post. My impression is that you simply are trying to tell me that I wasn't there, that I wasn't in the unit. I don't know. I simply don't know how to behave, nor what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I explained to you, Mr. Galic, my purpose is that I believe that your first statement that you gave to the investigator was the right statement, in which you did not remember being on duty. Now, I understand that you're saying that this is your writing in this book and my purpose is simply to jog your memory that you can remember that when you completed those entries, they were not completed on the 13th, 14th and 15th of July. Is that possible, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not possible. The entries could be made only on the date indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you remember telling the investigator during your second interview, that is after you were shown the book on 13 July, that you still did not remember having been on duty on the 22nd of July? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I said that because I wasn't shown that date. Please, I appeal to you once again, I cannot remember. I couldn't remember until I was shown the document, the entry for that date. Believe me, I cannot remember all the dates, and that is why I said I don't know, I can't remember. If I could remember I would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let us move on --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your second interview you stated that you received the order to go to the forward command post in the evening of the 13th and then that interview you said you were more or less ready because "I was supposed to take my duties sometime in the following days." Do you recall saying that to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you testified yesterday, you testified that you were -- I understood from your statement that you were more or less ready, and I don't have the reference unfortunately right now, you testified that you were supposed to be -- that you testified that you were more or less ready and I quote, "Because I was supposed to take my duties sometime in the following days." My understanding when you read your statement that you were referring to the 22nd, but yesterday you said that you were supposed to be on duty on the 14th of July in the morning. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn't say that like that. According to the schedule, I should have been on duty on the 14th. I never said I was ready, that I had expected, that I was ready to go. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I will let the Trial Chamber, when they look at your statement later on. Now, yesterday, you said that you were supposed to be on duty on the 14th. Is this your testimony today, that were you supposed to be on duty on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, according to schedule, yes, and I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I'm saying is that this is the first time that you ever say this to anyone, that were you supposed to be on duty on the 14th. So my question now is: Are both the 14th of July and the 22nd of July official dates that you were supposed to be on duty or is there one that you were not supposed to be on duty?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are dates on which I was supposed to be on duty, on the basis of the plan of the duty work at the forward command post. I couldn't have gone there otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if that's the case, you, as the assistant chief of staff for personnel, I'm asking you if you -- because you say you were supposed to be on duty on both the 14th and the 22nd, I say if what you're saying today, how come you did not remember any of this in your first interview, if it's so clear today?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember now, on the basis of the documents shown to me in this institution, with all the information. And that is why in the first interview, I didn't know, and I'm saying again, in this courtroom, that I didn't know when I was on duty anywhere. I don't know whether you can take it against me if I say I don't remember. I didn't know. If I had known there would be no problem. I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'd like to suggest to you is that the circumstances you describe in your testimony, that of being woken up at 11.00 or 10.00 at night and being asked to replace someone and taking a car and going to the forward command post, that this is something that, based on your knowledge that you gave to the investigator in your first interview, it is something that you could not have forgotten, if indeed it had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the first interview with the investigator, this was not discussed. I didn't talk to him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my case, Mr. Galic, is that you filled in those entries of the 13, 14 and 15, while were you sitting in the Zvornik command. Now, we'll go to this fact together and getting back to the book on duty during your second interview you were asked about this book, I'm talking about the forward command post duty book. Do you recall being asked about a stamp appearing at the end of the book? And I'd like to turn to page 49 in B/C/S and 44 in English.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, if I may, the gentleman said that I wrote this report in the brigade command. This is something I cannot accept as an individual, as a human being, and I see that I have no means of proving this. There is no reason for me to lie about anything or to leave anything out. That is part of my personality, and I really appeal to you. I cannot grapple with such things any more, that I had written these things not where I should have but at some other location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, if you look at the page before you, on the screen, and this is a --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you recognise this stamp, which says that the book has 100 pages, and you also recognise the signature of Dragan Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, I need to remember everything that happened in Zvornik over a period of five years. Shall I look at the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The only thing I'm asking you to do -- yes, you can look at the notebook indeed. The only thing I'm asking to you do is to remember that the investigator showed you the stamp and that your answer was, although you did not deal very much with the administration of correspondence, it was normal for such logbooks to have this kind of stamp at the end. Do you recall that the investigator showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He showed it to me, yes, but not at the first interview but at the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, second interview. Now, I suggest to you that you cannot explain, however --?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on the e-court. I don't think the witness should necessarily see the real book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's in the real book too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Both are there. You can look at the screen or the notebook or the original, as you wish. There is no need to look at the -- now, what I'd like to say, Mr. Galic, is that you cannot explain however why it says that this book contains 100 pages when in fact no matter how you count the pages, it does not add up to 100. I take it you cannot explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a misstatement of the evidence. And these continual personal challenges, could we give him a break and start this up again tomorrow? He's had a very long day and especially if we are going to go on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can probably finish in 15 minutes but maybe it's better to give the witness a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you have belaboured the point repeatedly, and the position of the witness has been constantly -- so I would suggest that you perhaps can now conclude on this part. And then we adjourn and start with something new tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, everything I have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I address the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness tried to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Galic, let me -- it's obvious, pretty obvious, that we are not going to finish today, also because Mr. McCloskey has got a set of questions to put to you and we've only got about ten minutes left so at this point in time, I'm suggesting to you, if you agree to it, that ten minutes, 12 minutes, won't make a difference. We can send you back to your hotel now. You will have a good rest, because tomorrow you're testifying in the morning and not in the afternoon. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree, but on the basis of yesterday's hearing and today, I had expected to finish today. I am a sick man with heart problems. I had my medicines up to today. And I don't wish to use anything else. I had hoped to finish today so that I could leave tomorrow and continue my medication. However, my understanding yesterday was that we would be finishing today, but the situation is as it is. Now, whether you care about my health or not, of course, it's up to you to decide what we should do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We certainly do care about your health. I want to put your mind at rest, that that tops the list of our concerns in such case. On the other hand, we have a procedure to follow here, and the procedure is such that although you might feel perhaps in your mind persecuted by Mr. Bourgon in putting all these questions to you, it's not the case. The case, the system that we have here, which we like to refer to as the adversarial system, encumbers, burdens, each Defence lawyer with a very heavy task, and that is of trying to elicit from you all the information that he would seek, to require to get from you, with a view to contradicting some of your evidence, some of your previous statements, and also to support the case that the -- each of the Defence teams might have. So I ask you to be patient because this is the system, this is the system. We can't conclude your testimony today. What I suggest is that if the Victims and Witnesses Section can procure the medication for you from your country by the speediest way possible, I wouldn't mention which service, that would be ideal because you would have it early tomorrow. On the other hand, I'm sure that the same medicine can be obtained here under a different brand name, and perhaps that could be arranged too. I'm pretty sure that the -- we have got very qualified persons in the Victims and Witnesses Unit who can help you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully. Thank you. I don't need any assistance. I'll bear it out for as long as I can. I hope I won't follow in the footsteps of Bojanic, Maric and others. I will prevail. I will manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't. Relax. Go to your hotel and make sure that you rest so that tomorrow you can come here and hopefully finish in good time to enable to you return home the earliest possible. On the other hand, may we again appeal to you, Mr. Bourgon, to please try to bring your cross-examination to an end? There are some points that of course you have every right to task the witness upon, but on the other hand, belabouring the same point over and over again when the position doesn't seem to change could become -- could be misunderstood, let me clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully understand, Mr. President. I simply have a few issues to put to the witness. I'm confident I will be able to jog his memory and he will remember differently but those are issues I will do very quickly tomorrow morning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Usher, you can escort the witness. Witness, we'll see you tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
